title: Bereshit: why begin with bet?
hook: the Torah opens with its second letter, closed on three sides and open ahead (Genesis Rabbah 1:10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, aliyah: going up to the scroll to bless before and after. Your line was go up. That finished the week on how the portion works. Now we open the first portion. Day one hundred sixty-one.

Every alphabet starts somewhere. English starts with A. Hebrew starts with aleph. So you might expect the Torah to start with aleph. It doesn't. The very first word of the Torah is Bereshit, in the beginning, and it starts with the second letter, bet. The rabbis noticed, and asked. Why would the Torah skip its own first letter? It seems like a tiny thing. But in the study hall, a tiny thing is a door. Today, the first portion begins, and we start by looking at one letter.
screen: `A, ALEPH, THE FIRST LETTER.` → `THE TORAH STARTS WITH BET.` → `A TINY THING IS A DOOR.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in English: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In Hebrew, the first word is Bereshit, and its first letter is bet. Look at the shape of a bet. It's like a square bracket: a line along the top, a line down the right side, a line along the bottom. And open on the left. Hebrew reads right to left, so that open side faces forward, into the rest of the text. The midrash, Genesis Rabbah, puts it this way. Why was the world created with a bet? Because just as the bet is closed on three sides and open on one, so you are not meant to ask what is above, what is below, what came before. Only from the day the world was created, and onward. That's a surprising answer. It sets a limit: some questions, about what came before the beginning, are closed. But it opens a road: everything after is yours to explore. The same passage offers another reason. Bet begins the word bracha, blessing. Aleph begins a word for curse. So the Torah starts with the letter of blessing. And Rashi, whom you met last week, adds a grammar puzzle. He says the first words don't quite mean, in the beginning. They mean something closer to, in the beginning of God's creating. Read that way, the verse isn't listing what was made first; it's the start of a longer sentence. So the Torah opens mid-sentence, with a letter that looks forward. The midrash puts the lesson in the letter's shape: a wall behind, and the way open ahead.
screen: `THE FIRST LETTER IS BET.` · `CLOSED ON THREE SIDES, OPEN AHEAD.` · `BET FOR BLESSING.` · `IN THE BEGINNING OF CREATING.` · then, large: `OPEN AHEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face forward. Settle, and breathe. Picture the letter bet: a roof, a wall behind you, a floor, and an open side in front. Let the wall behind you be everything already done: yesterday's mistakes, old worries, what you can't change. Let it hold you up instead of pulling you back. Now look toward the open side. What's one step ahead of you today? Just one. The bell holds the time.
Bereshit. In the beginning: the first word of the Torah and the name of its first portion, starting with a bet, open ahead.
Your line: open ahead. Today, for one hour, don't look back at what's already happened. Look only at what's in front of you. Day one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Parashat Bereshit, Genesis 1:1–6:8, is read on the Shabbat after Simchat Torah, and students traditionally begin their study of it with Rashi's comments on the first verse.

fork.setup: you're a student in the study hall. you notice the Torah starts with bet, not aleph. what do you do?
options: ignore it; a letter is just a letter.
fork.reveal: the rabbis asked. their answer: bet is closed on three sides and open ahead, and it's the letter of blessing.

original.note: Hebrew: in the beginning; the Torah's first word, starting with the letter bet, ב.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Bible starts at the beginning of time.
what it means: it starts with a letter open to the front, a limit behind you and a road ahead.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah 1:10 on the shape of bet and bet for bracha; Rashi on 1:1 reads bereshit in construct, 'in the beginning of God's creating'.

sources.quoted: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

notes: Genesis Rabbah 1:10 (Rabbi Yonah in the name of Rabbi Levi): bet closed on three sides; 'you may not investigate what is above, below, before, behind'. The script simplifies to above, below, before. Also bet for bracha vs aleph for arirah (curse). Confirm.
Rashi on 1:1: reads 'bereshit bara' as 'in the beginning of the creation of'. Confirm the simplified rendering.
The outline's carry 'open ahead' leans on the open side; the midrash's main point is a limit on speculation. The script states both. Confirm balance.
Many modern translations follow Rashi's reading ('When God began to create'); not named, to avoid non-PD translations.

Editor pass: cut the superlative 'the most important book in Hebrew' and 'they noticed everything'; Rashi's construct reading no longer overstated as 'the world was already in motion' (Rashi's point is that the verse doesn't teach the order of creation); the narrator's closing advice now points back to the midrash.
